accuracy.evidence: Checked against NHS 'Children's teeth' (reviewed 30 June 2025): for ages 3 to 6, brush at least twice daily for about 2 minutes, last thing at night and at least one other time, a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste with 1,000 to 1,500 ppm fluoride, a smear for children up to 3, spit out and do not rinse ('if you rinse, the fluoride won't work as well'), small circular movements, brush gums and behind the teeth, supervise; children 7 and over can brush their own. The acid attack of up to an hour after anything sugary, and keeping sugar to mealtimes, are from the Oral Health Foundation (Stephan curve lesson) and NHS trust dental diet leaflets. The lab's model (each meal is one acid attack; a treat at a meal adds none, a treat between meals or after the bedtime brush adds one) is stated as a simplification in the adult text. Parameterised answers: 2*a gives 2 to 8, a+b gives 2 to 7, 3+a gives 3 to 6, a+a gives 2 to 8 at every corner.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the brushing slips dental advice warns about: brushing only the front (Every side predict; the outside comes clean and the inside and tops still show plaque; p1, challenge 'front'), more toothpaste is better (pea predict; a long stripe is refused and wiped; p5, m8, challenge 'more'), a quick brush (Two minutes predict; 'Finished?' before 2:00 names the parts still with plaque; m1, challenge 'fast'), rinsing (Spit predict; the Rinse card washes the fluoride glow off the tooth; p4, m5, challenge 'rinse'), eating after the bedtime brush (Have a biscuit card, Bedtime slot, challenge 'night'), sweets nibbled all day (Sweets predict, acid bars, m2, m4, challenge 'graze') and scrubbing hard (m6, challenge 'hard').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagbrush is about tooth brushing itself: four teeth seen from the outside, the inside and the chewing tops with plaque that rubs off under a dragged toothbrush, a press-and-hold toothpaste tube whose blob grows from smear to pea to stripe and is judged for a child and for a baby, a four-part mouth with a 2-minute timer, a bedtime order builder where rinsing fades a fluoride glow, and a day timeline of acid attacks where treats are dragged to mealtimes. The labs of 'Hygiene: washing away germs' (hand washing) and 'Visiting the doctor or dentist' (the visit) do none of this; the lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every flagship lab, including flagroad, whose order step it does not copy.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is found by doing: the outside comes clean and the view turns to the inside, still covered in plaque; the stripe is refused and wiped while the pea is accepted, then the baby's brush needs only a smear; 'Finished?' early names the parts still dirty and the clock shows how far from 2:00; tapping Rinse visibly washes the fluoride glow away; moving juice, sweets and a biscuit to meals drops the red acid bars from 6 to 3. Done messages confirm each rule after the task.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'Yes, the front is what shows' (the inside and tops still have plaque), 'Yes, lots is best' (a stripe is refused as too much), 'About 10 seconds' (each part alone takes 30 seconds of brushing to clean) and 'Yes, rinse it all out' (rinsing washes the fluoride off), plus 'One at a time, all day' for sweets (the acid bars count 6, not 3). The correct option is first in two of them and second in three.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions; each wrong option is tagged to its slip and names it: front ('The front is only one side'), more ('More toothpaste does not clean better'), fast ('A quick brush misses lots of plaque'), rinse ('Rinsing washes the fluoride off'), night ('Food or juice after it sits on your teeth all night'), graze ('Every sweet snack starts a new acid attack'), hard ('Scrubbing hard can hurt your gums') and times. In-lab feedback also names the slip: how many plaque spots are left on which side, too much for a baby, which parts still need brushing, which step comes before, and how many acid attacks a move makes.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (plaque, pea, spit, rinse, gums, acid) with one idea each; the adult text gives the NHS amounts, the fluoride level and the slips plainly; validate_lessons readability passes for both. Canvas banners are short ('Outside: brush off the yellow plaque', 'Tap step 1 of bedtime brushing', 'Acid attacks today: 6') and every action is announced through the live region.

no_filler.evidence: Every sentence teaches a step or a reason (every side, pea, smear for a baby, 2 minutes, spit not rinse, sugar at mealtimes, only water after the bedtime brush); no throat-clearing or template text; the content gate finds no filler phrase and under 12% overlap with any lesson, including 'Hygiene: washing away germs' and 'Types of Teeth'.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark themes: teeth, plaque and the brush are large; the three view pills, the smear/pea/stripe pictures and the four mouth parts with their clocks are readable; on a phone the day timeline switches to two rows of three so 'Breakfast' and 'After brushing' stay at full size; every task has big buttons under the canvas (Brush the next spot, Squeeze a little, Brush top left, Move juice).

accessibility.evidence: Everything can be done with buttons as well as drag or press-and-hold: Brush the next spot, Squeeze a little and Wipe it off, Brush each part and Finished?, a button for every bedtime card, and Move juice/sweets/biscuit buttons whose labels say where each treat is now. The canvas aria-label is updated with every action (spots left, toothpaste size, part being brushed, acid attack count, challenge question); the walk gate's axe run finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark on desktop and phone.
